newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian culture minister sees more cash problems.
newsitem.headline: Russian culture minister sees more cash problems.

text.p: Russia has pumped extra cash into some of its main theatres and museums to ensure they stay open this year but more funding problems loom on the horizon, Culture Minister Yevgeny Sidorov said on Wednesday.

The government bowed to protests from its cultural elite and went back on a decision to pay out only 35 percent of this year's culture budget of 2.5 trillion roubles (now worth $460 million). About 70 percent of the sum will now be released.
"There will be no closures. The Finance Ministry has already made a first tranche of money available," Sidorov told Reuters in an interview.
But he added: "The same problems could arise (next year) if the budget is not paid out regularly every quarter."

Russian culture has suffered under a financial squeeze which has hit huge areas of the economy and meant workers in many industries have not been paid for months. The government has failed to meet many of its budget promises.

Russian artists, cherished stars of the former communist regime, now eke out a meagre living. Even Yevgeny Svetlanov, director of the State Symphony Orchestra, is said by fellow artists to earn only about 1.5 million roubles ($277) a month.

Leading artists took to the streets in Moscow last Friday to protest over cuts which they said could force institutions such as the Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg and the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow into bankruptcy.
They said salaries had not been paid, repairs were not being carried out and bills for electricity, water and security could not be met.
At Moscow's Russian State Library, formerly the Lenin Library, the average monthly wage is just 400,000 roubles ($74).

A spokeswoman told Reuters the library might be forced to cut its working houurs if wages were late. "Some employees might leave. We have many single mothers working here and they need money to feed their children."
It was a similar story at the Russian National Library in St Petersburg, where heating was recently cut off and some telephones said to have been disconnected to save money.

"Give us those pennies which you promised us," pianist Nikolai Petrov urged the goverment at Friday's protest, which began to the sombre tunes of Frederic Chopin's "Funeral March" to signal the misery of the arts in Russia.
In his interview, Sidorov said such protests had helped him to argue his case with the government, hinting that Russia would not have allowed its cultural jewels to close their doors.
"The talk about closures were some sort of blackmail, to frighten the state -- and the state got frightened," he said.
"Do you really think we would have let the Hermitage close, a museum which had been kept open all through the war, when bombs were flying around?"

Even so, the government was not ready to hand out all the money initially envisaged for culture in this year's budget. Sidorov said he expected about 70 percent of the budget would eventually be paid out. "Inshallah (God willing)," he said.
He said troubles were far from over for Russian culture and artists, who traditionally rely heavily on state financing and have had a tough time since the start of market reforms five years ago.
Sidorov said he was asking for about 2.7 trillion roubles ($500 million) in next year's budget -- one percent of total government spending.

The minister said 1996 had been the worst year for Russia's state-financed art sphere since the end of communist rule in 1991. Some restoration work had been cancelled as well as some theatre performances and festivals.
"But not a single cultural institution has been closed and we won't let that happen," he said.
